name: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and Maternal Thyroid Dysfunction

reference.source: Sakshi Arora Obstetrics 9th Edition / FIGO Guidelines on GDM
clinicalPearls: Human placental lactogen and maternal cortisol induce progressive peripheral insulin resistance peaking in the third trimester
DIPSI single-step non-fasting 75g oral glucose challenge diagnoses GDM if 2-hour venous plasma glucose is >= 140 mg/dL
Fetal hyperinsulinemia driven by maternal hyperglycemia triggers macrosomia and inhibits pulmonary surfactant synthesis
Maternal overt hypothyroidism increases risk of fetal neurocognitive impairment and requires a thirty to fifty percent dose increase
Target fasting blood glucose in GDM is below 95 mg/dL with 1-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL
reference.pathophysiology: Gestational diabetes results from pancreatic beta-cell inadequacy in meeting the metabolic demands of pregnancy. Placental hormones (hPL, progesterone, cortisol, growth hormone, TNF-alpha) cause post-receptor insulin receptor substrate-1 downregulation, generating physiological insulin resistance. Excess maternal glucose freely crosses the placenta via facilitated GLUT1 diffusion, triggering fetal hyperinsulinemia that accelerates fat deposition and suppresses type II pneumocyte surfactant production.
additionalDifferentials: Pre-existing overt type 2 diabetes versus gestational diabetes
Transient gestational hyperthyroidism of hyperemesis versus Graves disease
Subclinical hypothyroidism versus euthyroid autoimmune thyroiditis
additionalInvestigations: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks (or earlier if high risk)
Serum TSH and free T4 in early pregnancy
Fetal growth and liquor volume ultrasound surveillance every 3 to 4 weeks
Continuous blood glucose monitoring or daily self-monitoring
